name: First-degree murder
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Homicide
punishment_note: Death or life imprisonment without parole, as the court decides under the sentencing procedure in G.S. 15A-2000. Separate sentencing rules apply if the person was under 18 at the time.
explain_like_5: Someone caused another person's death on purpose after planning it, or while doing another very serious crime. This is the most serious kind of murder.
aliases: murder; premeditated murder; planned killing; felony murder
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-17(a), (a1), (c). Means, listed felonies, class, punishment and under-18 rule match. Malice and premeditation/deliberation meanings come from case law and the pattern jury instructions, not from the statute.
special_rules_text: G.S. 14-17(a1): if the murder was committed with malice against a spouse, former spouse, someone the person lives or lived with as if married, someone the person is or was in a dating relationship with, or someone the person shares a child with, and the person has an earlier conviction involving the same victim for domestic violence, violating a domestic violence protective order, communicating a threat, stalking, cyberstalking, or domestic criminal trespass, the law presumes the killing was willful, deliberate and premeditated. The presumption can be rebutted. If it holds, the murder is first-degree. | Felony-murder route: the person must have committed or tried to commit the underlying felony and meant to commit it. Malice and intent to kill aren't separate requirements on this route (N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.15, as summarized). | G.S. 14-17(c): a child born alive who dies from injuries inflicted before birth, or from an intentional, overt act after birth, can be the victim of murder. The degree is decided by the same rules. | Killing an unborn child is a separate offense under G.S. 14-23.2. It isn't covered in this tool yet.

name: Second-degree murder
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Homicide
punishment_note: Class B1 felony; Class B2 felony in the inherently dangerous act form.
explain_like_5: Someone caused another person's death and meant to hurt them badly, or acted with no care at all for human life, but didn't plan it ahead of time.
aliases: murder; killing
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-17(b), (c). Class B1/B2 and the B2 condition match after adding 'or omission' and the 'social duty and deliberately bent on mischief' wording. 14-23.2 exclusion added as a note.
special_rules_text: G.S. 14-17(c): a child born alive who dies from injuries inflicted before birth, or from an intentional, overt act after birth, can be the victim of murder. The degree is decided by the same rules. | Second-degree murder is defined by exclusion: a murder that isn't first-degree under 14-17(a) or (a1), and isn't murder of an unborn child under G.S. 14-23.2 (14-17(b)). The statute doesn't define malice; the meaning comes from court decisions.

name: Voluntary manslaughter
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Homicide
explain_like_5: Someone did something deliberate and dangerous that killed another person, but without malice: they acted in a sudden violent passion after being badly provoked, or used too much force defending themselves, or started a fight without meaning to kill. They didn't have to mean to kill.
aliases: manslaughter; killing; heat of passion
comparison_note: G.S. 14-18 sets punishment only (voluntary Class D, involuntary Class F) and matches. The statute doesn't define the offense, so the elements rest on case law and N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206 and cannot be verified against statute text.
special_rules_text: Intent to kill isn't required. 'Intentional' means the act was done on purpose and was an assault that is itself a felony or likely to cause death or serious injury (N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, n.21). | In a murder case the State must disprove heat of passion and self-defense. If it can't, the most that remains is voluntary manslaughter (206.10).

name: Involuntary manslaughter
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Homicide
explain_like_5: Someone caused another person's death without meaning to, through a lesser unlawful act (not a felony) or through carelessness so serious it showed no concern for other people's safety. It wasn't the kind of dangerous act that makes a killing voluntary manslaughter.
aliases: manslaughter; accidental killing; accidental death; negligent killing
comparison_note: G.S. 14-18 sets punishment only (voluntary Class D, involuntary Class F) and matches. The statute doesn't define the offense, so the elements rest on case law and N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206 and cannot be verified against statute text.
special_rules_text: The act can be intentional or not, but it can't itself be a felony or likely to result in death or great bodily harm. An act like that, done in passion or imperfect self-defense, is voluntary manslaughter, never involuntary (N.C.P.I.-Crim. 206.10, n.21). | If the death was an accident, with no wrongful purpose or criminal negligence, the person is not guilty (206.10).

name: First-degree burglary
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the habitation and other buildings > Burglary and breaking or entering
punishment_note: Class D felony. If the person had a firearm on their person during the offense, the sentence is one class higher (G.S. 14-52(b); offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025).
explain_like_5: Someone broke into and went inside someone else's home, planning to commit a serious crime or steal, while a person was inside.
aliases: burglary; break-in; breaking into a house; home break-in
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-51(a) and 14-52 as amended by S.L. 2025-71 (effective Dec 1, 2025). Removed the nighttime element, made the home 'of another', corrected the class-enhancement wording. N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10 (2011) predates the rewrite.
special_rules_text: Law changed Dec 1, 2025. S.L. 2025-71, s. 10(a) rewrote G.S. 14-51. The old text said burglary was 'as defined at the common law'; the new text spells out the offense and doesn't mention nighttime. This record follows the current text and applies to offenses committed on or after Dec 1, 2025. For earlier offenses the old law applies, and N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10 (dated 2011) lists a nighttime element. | The statute says 'any person is in the actual occupation of any part of' the home or sleeping room. That is what separates first-degree from second-degree burglary.

name: Second-degree burglary
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the habitation and other buildings > Burglary and breaking or entering
punishment_note: Class G felony. If the person had a firearm on their person during the offense, the sentence is one class higher (G.S. 14-52(b); offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025).
explain_like_5: The same as first-degree burglary, except nobody was inside when it happened.
aliases: burglary; break-in
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-51(b) and 14-52. Removed nighttime; dropped the curtilage/sleeping-room-in-another-building reach, which the current text doesn't name.
special_rules_text: Law changed Dec 1, 2025. S.L. 2025-71, s. 10(a) rewrote G.S. 14-51. The old text said burglary was 'as defined at the common law'; the new text spells out the offense and doesn't mention nighttime. This record follows the current text and applies to offenses committed on or after Dec 1, 2025. For earlier offenses the old law applies, and N.C.P.I.-Crim. 214.10 (dated 2011) lists a nighttime element. | Second-degree burglary needs no one actually inside. The old text also reached a house within the curtilage of a dwelling and a building that isn't a dwelling but has a sleeping room; the current text of 14-51(b) names only the dwelling house or sleeping room 'of another'.

name: Felony breaking or entering
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the habitation and other buildings > Burglary and breaking or entering
punishment_note: Class H felony. If the person had a firearm on their person during the offense, the sentence is one class higher (G.S. 14-54(b2); offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025).
explain_like_5: Someone broke into or went into a building planning to steal or commit another crime inside, or to scare or hurt someone there.
aliases: break-in; b&e; breaking into a building
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-54(a), (a1), (b2), (c). Class H and elements match. Special rule about daytime break-ins rewritten for the Dec 1, 2025 change to burglary.
special_rules_text: A break-in of a home with intent to commit a felony or larceny can fit both burglary (G.S. 14-51) and felonious breaking or entering (14-54(a)). Burglary needs both a breaking and an entering of a home or sleeping room 'of another'; felonious breaking or entering needs only a breaking or an entering, of any building. | Before Dec 1, 2025, a daytime break-in of a home landed here instead of burglary, because burglary required nighttime. S.L. 2025-71 removed that distinction from the statute's text.

name: Misdemeanor breaking or entering
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the habitation and other buildings > Burglary and breaking or entering
punishment_note: Class 1 misdemeanor. If the person had a firearm on their person during the offense, the sentence is one class higher (G.S. 14-54(b2); offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025).
explain_like_5: Someone broke into or went into a building without permission, without a plan to steal or hurt anyone.
aliases: break-in; b&e; entering a building
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-54(b), (b1), (b2). Class 1 matches. (b1) note updated with the Class I felony for repeat offenses.
special_rules_text: G.S. 14-54(b1), added by S.L. 2025-71 (offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025), separately covers entering a back-of-store area or a marked 'no entry' area with intent to commit an unlawful act: Class 1 misdemeanor, Class I felony for a second or later offense. Not modeled yet. | A firearm on the person raises the class by one (G.S. 14-54(b2)).

name: Felony larceny
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against property > Larceny
punishment_note: Class H felony (14-72(a)). If the larceny is of mail, one class level higher (14-72(c1)).
explain_like_5: Someone took something that belonged to another person and meant to keep it, and either it was worth more than $1,000 or the way it was taken made it more serious, like taking it from a person or taking a gun.
aliases: theft; stealing; steal
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-72(a)-(c1). Class H, the $1,000 line and the jury-sets-value rule match. The felony-circumstance list was incomplete (State Archives records missing; 'several' earlier convictions is four; 'burglary or B&E' covers 14-51, 14-53, 14-54, 14-54.1, 14-57). Fixed. The meaning of larceny itself (the taking) comes from case law and N.C.P.I.-Crim. 216, not from the statute.
special_rules_text: G.S. 14-72 also covers receiving or possessing stolen goods knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe they are stolen, with the same value and circumstance rules (Class H over $1,000 or in a (b) circumstance, otherwise Class 1 misdemeanor). Not modeled yet. | Mail: if the larceny is of mail, the sentence is one class level higher than the principal offense (14-72(c1); added by S.L. 2025-71, s. 9, for offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025). Not modeled as its own offense. | Other larceny-type offenses exist in other sections, such as larceny of gift cards (G.S. 14-72.12, added by S.L. 2025-71 for offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025) and retail theft offenses. Not modeled yet.

name: Misdemeanor larceny
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against property > Larceny
punishment_note: Class 1 misdemeanor (14-72(a)). If the larceny is of mail, one class level higher (14-72(c1)).
explain_like_5: Someone took something that belonged to another person and meant to keep it, and it was worth $1,000 or less.
aliases: theft; stealing; petty theft; steal
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-72(a). Class 1 misdemeanor and the $1,000 line match; added the rule that a (b) circumstance makes it a felony whatever the value.
special_rules_text: Misdemeanor larceny applies 'except as provided in subsections (b) and (c)': if any felony circumstance in 14-72(b) applies, it is felony larceny even when the value is $1,000 or less. | If the larceny is of mail, the sentence is one class level higher (14-72(c1); offenses on or after Dec 1, 2025).

name: Assault with a deadly weapon in a secret manner with intent to kill
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone lay in wait or otherwise attacked a person in a hidden way, with a deadly weapon, meaning to kill.
aliases: ambush; waylaying; lying in wait assault
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-31 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.
special_rules_text: The victim having been aware of the attacker's presence does not take the case out of the statute.

name: Assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill, inflicting serious injury
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone attacked another person with a deadly weapon, meaning to kill them, and seriously hurt them.
aliases: stabbing; shooting; assault with a weapon
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32(a). Elements and Class C match. Serious injury and deadly weapon meanings come from case law and the pattern instructions; the statute defines neither.

name: Assault with a deadly weapon inflicting serious injury
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone attacked another person with a deadly weapon and seriously hurt them. They didn't have to mean to kill.
aliases: stabbing; shooting; assault with a weapon; AWDWISI
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32(b). Elements and Class E match; the statute lists no intent-to-kill element.
special_rules_text: No intent to kill is required. The statute lists none.

name: Assault with a deadly weapon with intent to kill
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone attacked another person with a deadly weapon, meaning to kill them. The victim didn't have to be seriously hurt.
aliases: assault with a weapon; AWDWIK
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32(c). Elements and Class E match; the statute lists no injury element.
special_rules_text: No injury is required. The statute lists none.

name: Assault inflicting serious bodily injury
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone attacked another person and caused a life-threatening or lasting injury, and no other law punishes it more.
aliases: badly hurting someone; serious injury assault
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32.4(a). Elements, the 'unless covered by a law with greater punishment' limit, the Class F class and the definition of serious bodily injury match. Tightened the definition to say 'protracted' means long-lasting and that impairment of function counts.
special_rules_text: Not the same as 'serious injury' in G.S. 14-32 and 14-33. 'Serious bodily injury' has its own statutory definition.

name: Assault inflicting physical injury by strangulation
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone attacked another person and hurt them by strangling them, and no other law punishes it more.
aliases: choking; strangling
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32.4(b). Elements, the greater-punishment limit and Class H match. What counts as strangulation and as physical injury comes from the pattern instruction and an unpublished decision, not the statute.

name: Simple assault
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone threatened or hit another person, without a weapon, without seriously hurting them, and without the victim being in a specially protected group.
aliases: fight; hitting someone; punching; battery; affray
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-33(a). Class 2 matches. The statute doesn't define assault, so that meaning rests on case law and N.C.P.I.-Crim. 120.20.
special_rules_text: Also covers simple assault and battery and simple affray. No weapon, injury, or victim category is required.

name: Aggravated assault (Class A1 misdemeanor)
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone assaulted another person, and either seriously hurt them, used a deadly weapon, or the victim was in a group the law gives extra protection.
aliases: aggravated assault; assault on a woman; assault on a child
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-33(c). All nine victim or conduct categories, the greater-punishment limit and Class A1 match. Expanded the school-worker definition (contractors, supervised volunteers, what counts as duties). The attempt wording in a 2002 instruction is not in the current statute.
special_rules_text: North Carolina's statute headings call this 'aggravated assault, assault and battery, or affray', but it is a misdemeanor. In many other states, 'aggravated assault' is a felony. | Using a deadly weapon, or causing serious injury, makes it this offense at the misdemeanor level. The felony assault offenses in G.S. 14-32 add further elements. | A 2002 pattern instruction (208.55) also lists 'attempting to inflict serious injury' under this subsection. The current text of G.S. 14-33(c)(1), read on 2026-10-17, says 'inflicts serious injury upon another person or uses a deadly weapon', so the attempt wording isn't followed here. | If a man is also convicted of a higher-class assault for the same conduct, a court should arrest judgment on assault on a female (N.C.P.I.-Crim. 208.70, n.1, citing an unpublished case). | G.S. 14-33(c1) protects school personnel who take reasonable good-faith action to end a fight between students from civil or criminal liability. It is not an element of any offense.

name: Habitual misdemeanor assault
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone committed a new misdemeanor assault that caused injury, or domestic violence or pointing a gun, after at least two earlier assault convictions in the last 15 years.
aliases: repeat assault; habitual assault
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-33.2 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.
special_rules_text: A conviction under this section can't be used as a prior conviction for any other habitual offense statute. | Amended by S.L. 2025-70, s. 17(b), effective for offenses committed on or after Dec 1, 2025.

name: Assault by pointing a gun
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Everyday assault
explain_like_5: Someone pointed a gun at another person. It doesn't matter if it was a joke or if the gun wasn't loaded.
aliases: pointing a gun; gun; waving a gun
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-34. Elements and Class A1 match. The statute has no intent word and lists no exceptions; the word 'intentionally' in the plain wording comes from the pattern instruction.
special_rules_text: Applies 'in fun or otherwise', and whether or not the gun is loaded. No injury is required. The statute's text lists no exceptions, though courts may recognize defenses that aren't modeled here.

name: Assault on an emergency worker with a deadly weapon inflicting serious injury
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone attacked a police officer, firefighter, EMT, or medical responder with a deadly weapon and seriously hurt them.
aliases: assaulting an officer; assault on a police officer; assault on a firefighter
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32(d) and (f). Elements and Class D match. Added the note that the four groups in (f) are undefined.
special_rules_text: 'Emergency worker' is limited to the four groups named in G.S. 14-32(f): law enforcement officer, firefighter, emergency medical technician, medical responder. The statute defines none of them.

name: Assault on an emergency worker with a deadly weapon with intent to kill
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone attacked a police officer, firefighter, EMT, or medical responder with a deadly weapon, meaning to kill them.
aliases: assaulting an officer; assault on a police officer; assault on a firefighter
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-32(e) and (f). Elements and Class D match.
special_rules_text: 'Emergency worker' is limited to the four groups named in G.S. 14-32(f). The statute defines none of them. | If serious injury was also inflicted, other parts of G.S. 14-32 may fit the same conduct too (for example (a) or (d)). This record doesn't model how those overlap.

name: Aggravated assault on a sports official or utility worker (Class 1 misdemeanor)
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone assaulted a referee, umpire, or coach at a sports event, or a utility or phone or internet worker doing their job.
aliases: aggravated assault; assault on a referee; assault on an umpire
comparison_note: Compared with full text of G.S. 14-33(b). Both remaining subdivisions, the greater-punishment limit and Class 1 match. Fixed the utility-worker definition (it covers liquid petroleum, agents and contractors, and 'readily identifiable' is not limited to logo clothing) and broadened the sports-official definition.
special_rules_text: The older subdivisions of G.S. 14-33(b) have been repealed. Only (9) sports official and (10) utility or communications worker remain. | Subdivision (10), the utility or communications worker, was added by S.L. 2025-71, s. 1(a), and applies to offenses committed on or after Dec 1, 2025.

name: Assault with a deadly weapon on a government officer or employee, company or campus police officer
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone assaulted a government officer or employee, or a company or campus police officer, with a deadly weapon while they were doing their job.
aliases: assault on a government employee with a weapon
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-34.2 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.
special_rules_text: The victim must be performing an official duty.

name: Assault with a firearm on an officer, National Guard member or detention employee
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone assaulted a police, probation or parole officer, a National Guard member, or a jail or prison employee with a firearm while they were doing their job.
aliases: assault on an officer with a gun
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-34.5 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.
special_rules_text: G.S. 14-34.5 has no 'unless covered by a law with greater punishment' limit.

name: Assault or affray causing physical injury to a health care worker, firefighter or hospital worker

explain_like_5: Someone hurt an EMT, firefighter, hospital worker or similar person who was doing their job.
aliases: assault on a nurse; assault on a firefighter; assault on EMS; assault on hospital staff

special_rules_text: Using a deadly weapon other than a firearm, or inflicting serious bodily injury, raises it to Class F under subsection (b). Using a firearm raises it to Class D under subsection (c). | Subdivision (a)(4) was repealed in 2011.

name: Assault on a health care worker, firefighter or hospital worker causing serious bodily injury or with a non-firearm deadly weapon
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone seriously hurt an EMT, firefighter or hospital worker doing their job, or attacked them with a deadly weapon that wasn't a firearm.
aliases: assault on a nurse with a weapon
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-34.6 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.

name: Assault on a health care worker, firefighter or hospital worker using a firearm
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone used a firearm in an assault that hurt an EMT, firefighter or hospital worker doing their job.
aliases: assault on a nurse with a gun
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-34.6 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.

name: Assault inflicting serious bodily injury on an officer, National Guard member or detention employee
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone seriously hurt a police, probation or parole officer, a National Guard member, or a jail or prison employee who was doing their job.
aliases: assault on an officer serious injury

where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone hurt a police, probation or parole officer, a National Guard member, or a jail or prison employee who was doing their job, even with only cuts, scrapes or bruises.

comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-34.7 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.

name: Pointing a laser at an officer or other listed worker on duty
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Assault on officers and workers on duty
explain_like_5: Someone intentionally pointed a laser at a police officer, firefighter, EMT, guard or another listed worker doing their job.
aliases: laser pointer at police; laser at a pilot

name: Misdemeanor crime of domestic violence
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Domestic violence
explain_like_5: Someone used or tried to use force, or threatened to use a deadly weapon, against a partner, former partner, co-parent or family member covered by the law.
aliases: domestic violence; DV; domestic assault
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-32.5 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.
special_rules_text: Unlike the assault offenses, this one is defined by the relationship and by force or a threatened deadly weapon, not by assault or injury. | A conviction under G.S. 14-33 is not a lesser included offense of this crime (G.S. 14-33(e)). | The relationship list here is not the same as the 'personal relationship' list in G.S. 50B-1(b), which G.S. 14-33(d) uses.

name: Habitual domestic violence
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Domestic violence
punishment_note: Class H felony for the first offense. Each later conviction under this section is one class higher than the most recent prior conviction under it, up to Class C.
explain_like_5: Someone committed another domestic violence offense after at least two earlier qualifying convictions in the last 15 years.
aliases: repeat domestic violence
comparison_note: Drafted from the full text of G.S. 14-32.6 read on 2026-10-17. No pattern jury instruction was compared for this record. Terms the statute leaves undefined are flagged on the elements.
special_rules_text: A conviction under this section can't be used as a prior conviction for any other habitual offense statute (G.S. 14-32.6(b)). | The relationships are those listed in G.S. 14-32.5. | G.S. 14-32.6 was added by S.L. 2025-70, s. 18(a).

name: Assault in the presence of a minor against a person with a personal relationship
where_in_statute_tree: Offenses against the person > Assaults > Domestic violence
punishment_note: Class A1 misdemeanor. If community punishment is imposed, supervised probation is required. A second or later offense requires an active sentence of at least 30 days.
